hints: Think about what the Calvin cycle needs besides ATP and carbon dioxide - it needs a source of hydrogen and electrons to make a more energy-rich molecule.
Focus on the reduction step in the middle of the cycle - which 3-carbon acid is converted into which 3-carbon sugar phosphate using reduced NADP?
walkthrough:
Link Light Dependent to Light Independent**
Reduced NADP is made in the light dependent reaction and carries hydrogen and high-energy electrons to the stroma for the Calvin cycle. Think of it as the reducing power.

Pinpoint the Reduction Reaction**
In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide fixed to RuBP forms GP. Reduced NADP then donates its hydrogen to reduce GP to TP, becoming oxidised back to NADP in the process.
Final answer: Reduced NADP reduces glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) to triose phosphate (TP).

hints: If DCPIP takes the hydrogen instead of NADP, follow what is missing downstream - can GP still be reduced to TP, and can RuBP still be remade?
walkthrough:
Trace the Block**
If DCPIP is reduced instead of NADP, no reduced NADP is available. Without reduced NADP, GP cannot be reduced to TP.

Effect on RuBP**
TP is needed to regenerate RuBP. RuBP continues to react with carbon dioxide in carbon fixation but is not replaced, so its concentration falls.
Final answer: RuBP concentration decreases as RuBP is used up in carbon fixation but is not regenerated.

hints: Think about why judging colour change by eye is difficult - what fixed reference would let you decide exactly when the blue colour has gone?
Consider what tube B contains and what would happen to it if left on the bench in the light before the timed test starts.
Remember DCPIP only decolourises when the light dependent reaction runs - what does foil do to light entry and electron flow?
Link the two ideas together - how does keeping the stock mixture dark ensure every wavelength test starts fairly from the same point?
walkthrough:
Why Tube A Is Needed**
Tube A contains chloroplast suspension without blue DCPIP, so it shows the final colourless-green end-point. You compare tube B against it to judge exactly when all DCPIP has been reduced, giving a consistent, objective timing point.

Why Foil Is Needed**
The beaker holds the stock chloroplast-DCPIP mixture for future tests. Foil and a foil lid block light from reaching chlorophyll, which prevents the light dependent reaction and premature reduction and decolourising of DCPIP.

Fair Start for All Colours**
This means every fresh tube B starts with the same blue colour and same unreduced DCPIP concentration, so differences in time to decolourise are due to wavelength only.

Final answer: Tube A provides a colour standard for comparison to judge the end-point when all DCPIP in B has been reduced. Foil stops/limits light entering to stop/limit the light dependent reaction and DCPIP decolourising, so all tests start with the same colour.

hints: Look at the formula $rate = \frac{1000}{t}$ and pick out the correct $t$ value for orange light from Table 2.1 before dividing.
walkthrough:
Substitute and Calculate**
For orange light $t = 45 \text{ s}$. So $rate = \frac{1000}{45} = 22.22...$ which rounds to $22.2 \text{ s}^{-1}$, matching the one decimal place used in the table.

hints: Start by ranking the rates in Table 2.1 - which colour gives the shortest time and highest rate, and which gives the longest time and lowest rate?
Quote the key numbers with units to support your description, for example purple at 425 nm versus green at 525 nm.
Recall which wavelengths chlorophyll a and b absorb strongly and which they reflect - why would green be so slow?
Think about why there is still some activity in blue, orange and red - what other pigments help capture light?
Connect absorbed light to DCPIP decolourising - what happens to chlorophyll electrons that drives faster reduction of DCPIP?
walkthrough:
Describe the Pattern With Data**
Rate is highest in purple light at 425 nm with $27.0 \text{ s}^{-1}$ (time only 37 s) and also high in orange and red. Rate is lowest in green light at 525 nm with $2.1 \text{ s}^{-1}$ (time 480 s). Blue is intermediate at $11.9 \text{ s}^{-1}$.

Explain Absorption**
Chlorophyll absorbs purple/blue and orange/red light strongly but absorbs green very poorly and reflects it. That is why green drives the light dependent reaction so slowly. Accessory pigments such as carotenoids absorb some other wavelengths and pass energy to chlorophyll, so photosynthesis still occurs across the spectrum.

Link Light to DCPIP Reduction**
Absorbed photons excite electrons in photosystem reaction centres, triggering electron transport and non-cyclic photophosphorylation. More excitation means more electrons and hydrogen transferred to DCPIP per unit time, so faster decolourising. The plot of rate against wavelength is the action spectrum for the light dependent stage.

Final answer: Rate highest/fastest in purple at 425 nm (27.0 s-1) and lowest/slowest in green at 525 nm (2.1 s-1). Chlorophyll absorbs purple and orange/red best but does not absorb green; accessory pigments absorb other wavelengths; absorbed light excites electrons and drives electron transport/non-cyclic photophosphorylation, reducing DCPIP faster. This is the action spectrum.
